lead: Every line on a yacht has a job, and each job has its rope, its knot and a safe way to handle it. Let a cleat or a winch take the load your hands cannot.

sections.title: Stretch where you moor, none where you trim

qa.q: What rope should I use for mooring lines, and what for sheets and halyards?
qa.a: Use **nylon** for mooring lines and anchor warps: it stretches and absorbs shock loads. Sheets and halyards must not stretch, so they are polyester, or Dyneema for halyards.

head: Rope
Behaviour
Use
rows: Anchor warp, mooring and tow lines

blocks.p: A mooring line in a swell takes snatch loads many times the steady pull, so it must stretch; a sheet or a halyard must not. Load a rope to about a fifth of its **breaking strength** at most: knots, wear and shock use up the rest.

fig.note: A thimble inside the eye takes the chafe

blocks.p: A knot is the weakest point of a line, so a permanent loop is an **eye splice**, often round a **thimble**, a grooved metal ring. Three-strand rope is the easiest to splice by hand.

sections.title: Know each knot by its job

qa.q: What are the essential sailing knots, and what is each one used for?
qa.a: Tie a **bowline** for a fixed loop, a clove hitch for fenders, a round turn and two half hitches to a ring or post, a sheet bend to join two lines, and a figure of eight as a stopper.

blocks.p: A reef knot is right end over left and round, then left over right: it lies flat, each line's two parts side by side. The same way twice is a **granny**, which slips or jams. In a sheet bend the thicker line forms the bight. Slip a knot only on a line you are watching.

qa.q: How do I tie a line to a cleat properly?
qa.a: Lead the line to the far horn of the cleat, take a full turn round the base, add figure-of-eight turns and finish with one **locking hitch**: more only jam.

list: Lead the line to the far horn and take a full turn round the base.
Add two or three figure-of-eight turns.
Finish with one **locking hitch**; more only jam.

blocks.p: Keep the first turn on to ease a loaded line, and take one on any line too heavy to hold. When two lines share a cleat, the first to leave goes on top.

tiles.name: Making fast
tiles.note: turn, figures of eight, one hitch

blocks.p: Ashore, drop the loop over the bollard and adjust the line from the boat. Pass your loop up through another boat's loop first, so that either can leave. A **slip line** runs round the bollard with both ends aboard: let one go, pull in the other. No knots in it; rig it just before leaving, and have it all aboard before the propeller turns.

qa.q: Which way do the turns go on a winch, and how many do I need?
qa.a: Turns go on a winch **clockwise**: two to pull in slack, three or four as the load builds. Tension on the tail makes them grip.

blocks.p: Turns go on a winch **clockwise**: two to pull in slack, three or four as the load builds. Their friction holds the load; the tail only keeps them tight. A self-tailing winch takes the tail over the arm into its jaws last.

fig.note: Lead from slightly below the drum: no riding turns

list: Ease with the turns on and the tail out of the jaws.
Release by lifting all the turns off together, never one by one.
Riding turn: take the load on a spare line with a rolling hitch, then clear it.
Too heavy: turn the handle the other way for low gear.
Handle out when you finish. Hair and scarves clear. Stop an electric winch at any snag.

blocks.p: A **clutch** holds a line so the winch is free for the next. Check its label before opening it. To ease a loaded halyard, take the load on the winch, then open the clutch; after hoisting, close it before the turns come off. It grips only its own rope diameter. A cam cleat lets go when you pull in a little and lift.

sections.title: Keep yourself out of the line

qa.q: How do I throw a line so it actually reaches the person catching it?
qa.a: To **throw a line**, make the inboard end fast first, then split the coil, half to throw and half to pay out. Aim above and just beyond the catcher; for a long throw, send a light line first.

list: Never stand in a loop of line.
Hold a line in your hands, never wrapped round them; wear gloves.
Keep hands well back from blocks.
If a line runs away, let go, then catch it with a turn on a cleat.
No slack line in the water with the engine in gear.
Check that a tail is free to run before you release it.

fig.note: A parting line whips back: stand to one side

blocks.p: To **throw a line**, make the inboard end fast first. If it falls short, pull it in fast, clear of the propeller. For a long throw, send a light line first and haul the heavy one across.

qa.q: How do I coil a rope on a yacht so it doesn't twist?
qa.a: Coil three-strand rope **clockwise**, with the lay, and braid in figure-of-eight loops, which add no twist. Start from the fixed end so that twists run out of the free end.

blocks.p: Replace a sheet whose cover has worn through to the core. At night, tie halyards off away from the mast.
Coil three-strand rope **clockwise**, with the lay, and braid in figure-of-eight loops, which add no twist. Bind the coil and tuck the end through before stowing it.
